## codegraph
# Codegraph — code intelligence over an indexed knowledge graph

Codegraph is a SQLite knowledge graph of every symbol, edge, and file in
the workspace — pre-computed structure you would otherwise re-derive by
reading files (cached intelligence: thousands of parse/trace decisions you
don't pay to re-reason each run). Reads are sub-millisecond; the index lags
writes by ~1s through the file watcher. Reach for it BEFORE *and* while
writing or editing code — not just for questions: one call returns the
verbatim source PLUS who calls it and what it affects, so you edit with the
blast radius in view. More accurate context, in far fewer tokens and
round-trips than reading files yourself.

## One tool: codegraph_explore — use it instead of reading files

There is a single tool, `codegraph_explore`, and it is Read-equivalent. It
takes either a natural-language question or a bag of symbol/file names and
returns the **verbatim, line-numbered source** of the relevant symbols
grouped by file — the same `<n>\t<line>` shape `Read` gives you, safe to
`Edit` from — PLUS the call path among them (including dynamic-dispatch hops
like callbacks, React re-render, and JSX children that grep can't follow) and
a blast-radius summary of what depends on them.

Whether you're answering "how does X work" or implementing a change (fixing a
bug, adding a feature), call `codegraph_explore` before you Read. ONE call
usually answers the whole question. Codegraph IS the pre-built search index —
so running your own grep + read loop, or delegating the lookup to a separate
file-reading sub-task/agent, repeats work codegraph already did and costs more
for the same answer. A direct codegraph answer is typically one to a few
calls; a grep/read exploration is dozens.

**Premise correction:** There is no Redis anywhere in the cache layer. The repository (Memos) uses a **thread-safe in-process, in-memory Go cache** — a `sync.Map`-backed store with TTL expiration and a background cleanup goroutine. No external cache server, connection string, or Redis client is involved. (The word "cache" also appears in an unrelated browser-side editor draft cache in `web/src/components/MemoEditor/services/cacheService.ts`, which just uses `localStorage`, and in an RSS-feed cache in `server/router/rss/rss.go`, which is a separate ad-hoc map — neither is Redis either.)

**Actual mechanism:**

- **Cache implementation:** `store/cache/cache.go` — `Cache` is a `sync.Map` with per-item `expiration` timestamps (`item` struct, lines 34–39). `New(config)` (line 76) starts a `cleanupLoop` goroutine that periodically evicts expired entries. There is no connection to configure; it's created purely in memory.

- **Where it's "configured"/wired up:** `store/store.go`, `New()` (lines 38–61). The `Store` holds three caches — `instanceSettingCache`, `userCache`, and `userSettingCache` (lines 27–29) — each constructed via `cache.New(cacheConfig)` (lines 51–53). The config is defined inline at lines 40–45:
  - `DefaultTTL: 10 * time.Minute`
  - `CleanupInterval: 5 * time.Minute`
  - `MaxItems: 1000`

  (This mirrors `cache.DefaultConfig()` at `store/cache/cache.go:57`.)

- **TTL for user entries:** User records are cached in `userCache` keyed by user ID (`store/user.go`: `userCacheKey`, and `s.userCache.Set(...)` in `CreateUser`/`UpdateUser`/`ListUsers`/`GetUser`, lines 98, 132, 143, 167). Those `Set` calls use the default TTL — `Cache.Set` delegates to `SetWithTTL(..., c.config.DefaultTTL)` (`store/cache/cache.go:93–95`). So **user entries expire 10 minutes after they are written** (`DefaultTTL = 10 * time.Minute`, `store/store.go:41`). No code path uses `SetWithTTL` to give users a custom TTL, so 10 minutes applies uniformly. The same 10-minute default applies to the `userSettingCache` entries as well.
